2-31.why: II and IV are duplicates (scheduled job vs lifecycle rule); Bucket Lock has no extra charge and is the only option covering the 7-year retention requirement. Matches the same scenario in 1-2.
2-31.explanation:
**Correct Answers:**

  * **I. Apply the Bucket Lock feature to enforce a retention policy on the data.**

  * **IV. Establish a lifecycle management policy to transition objects older than 14 days to the Coldline storage class.**




**Justification:**

  * **Retention (I):** The stem requires keeping the data for at least 7 years. A bucket retention policy (locked with Bucket Lock) guarantees that no object can be deleted or overwritten before it reaches that age. Bucket Lock itself has no extra charge; you only pay for the storage you keep, which you would have to keep anyway.

  * **Tiering (IV):** Logs are reviewed often during the first two weeks, then only once a year. A lifecycle rule that moves objects older than 14 days to Coldline (designed for data accessed less than once a quarter) cuts storage cost, and it runs automatically with no code to maintain.




**Why Other Options Are Less Ideal:**

  * **II. Schedule a job to transition objects older than 14 days to the Coldline storage class.** This does the same thing as IV, but you have to write, schedule and monitor the job yourself. Object Lifecycle Management is the managed, declarative way to do it, and choosing both II and IV would leave the retention requirement unmet.

  * **III. Generate a JSON Web Token (JWT) for users requiring access to the Coldline storage buckets.** Access is handled with IAM; JWTs do nothing for cost or retention.

  * **V. Configure a lifecycle management policy to transition objects older than 14 days to the Nearline storage class.** Nearline suits data read about once a month. For data read once a year, Coldline is cheaper.

3-20.explanation:
**I. Establish distinct datasets for each department, and in each one create a view with the appropriate WHERE clause to filter the department's records from the "Master" dataset. Authorize these views to access records from the "Master" dataset, granting employees access to their respective departmental datasets.**

This is BigQuery's **authorized view** pattern:

  * **No data copies:** The data stays in the "Master" dataset. Each department dataset only holds a view that selects that department's rows.

  * **Access to the view, not the tables:** Authorizing the view on the "Master" dataset lets the view read the source tables on the users' behalf. Employees get access only to their department's dataset, so they can query the view without any permission on the "Master" tables.

  * **Separate dataset is required:** An authorized view must live in a different dataset from the source data. Putting the views in their own datasets is what keeps the base tables out of reach.

  * **Simple to manage:** Granting a team access to one dataset is one IAM binding, and changes in "Master" show up in the views immediately.




**Why Other Options Are Less Ideal:**

  * **II. Set up separate datasets for each department and implement data pipelines ...** This copies the data, adds storage cost, and adds pipelines to build and keep in sync.

  * **III. Create a "Master" dataset and develop individual views for each department within it ...** A view in the same dataset as its source can't be an authorized view. Without authorization, a user querying the view also needs read access to the underlying "Master" tables, which would expose every department's records.

  * **IV. Create a "Master" dataset and segregate data into separate tables for each department ...** Splitting the data into per-department tables complicates loading and cross-department queries, and you still have to manage table-level permissions inside the shared dataset.

6-6.explanation:
The correct answer is 

**A. Assign the roles/cloudsql.client role to the custom service account. Then, update the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy startup command with your instance connection name.**

Explanation:

Google's documentation says that a service account connecting through the **Cloud SQL Auth Proxy** needs the **Cloud SQL Client** role (`roles/cloudsql.client`). It is the predefined role made for this job: it lets the account connect to instances (and read the instance metadata the proxy needs) without letting it change or delete them, so it meets the **principle of least privilege** with no custom role to maintain.

The proxy then needs to know which instance to reach, so you start it with the **instance connection name** (`project:region:instance`). On Windows, the application connects to the proxy over TCP on localhost.

Justifications for Incorrect Options:

  * **Option B: Assign roles/cloudsql.client and use the --unix-socket option**  
The role is right, but Google's documentation states that Unix sockets aren't supported for the Windows environment. On a Windows VM you connect to the proxy over a TCP port instead.

  * **Option C: Grant the roles/cloudsql.editor role**  
The `roles/cloudsql.editor` role provides broad permissions, including modifying database instances, which violates the principle of least privilege and poses a security risk.

  * **Option D: Assign the roles/cloudsql.viewer role**  
The `roles/cloudsql.viewer` role allows read-only access to Cloud SQL resources but does not grant the `cloudsql.instances.connect` permission needed for the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy to establish a connection.




**Relevant Documentation:**

For more information, refer to:

  * [Using the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy](https://cloud.google.com/sql/docs/mysql/sql-proxy)

6-8.why: Backend is in one region, so the gain is edge termination on Premium Tier, not routing to the closest backend; passthrough NLB does carry HTTP.
explanation: 1. **Use an external Application Load Balancer** : Google Cloud's external **Application Load Balancer** is built on the **Premium Tier network** , offering global load balancing with proximity-based routing. This setup reduces latency by routing each request to the backend instance closest to the device, minimizing TTFB.

1. **Use an external Application Load Balancer** : With **Premium Tier**, the global external **Application Load Balancer** terminates the TCP and TLS connections at the Google edge location closest to each device, then carries the request to the backend over Google's private network. The backend is in a single region, so the gain doesn't come from picking a closer backend: it comes from shorter handshakes (connection setup happens near the device) and reused connections from the edge to the backend, which lowers TTFB.

The Network Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) and does not support HTTP(S) protocols natively. It also lacks advanced features like proximity-based routing, which is crucial for reducing TTFB for a geographically dispersed user base.

The passthrough Network Load Balancer is regional and operates at Layer 4: it forwards the HTTP traffic, but connections aren't terminated at the edge, so every TCP and TLS handshake travels all the way to the backend region. That gives a higher TTFB than the Application Load Balancer.

5-9.explanation:
The correct answer is

**D. Set up separate Cloud Run services for public and restricted microservices. Enable IAP only for restricted services, and set the Cloud Run ingress settings to 'Internal and Cloud Load Balancing' for these services.**

Explanation:

  1. **Public services** : Deployed as their own Cloud Run services with the `roles/run.invoker` role granted to `allUsers`, so anyone can call them with no sign-in.

  2. **Restricted services** : Put behind an external Application Load Balancer with **Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)** enabled, and grant the IAP-secured Web App User role only to the Google identities that need access.

  3. **Ingress 'Internal and Cloud Load Balancing'** : This setting still allows traffic that arrives through the external Application Load Balancer, but it blocks requests sent straight to the service's `run.app` URL. Users therefore can't bypass IAP.




This keeps each service's access rule simple and uses managed Google features only, with no custom code.

Justifications for Incorrect Options:

  * **Option A: Develop a new microservice to manage access**  
Writing your own access-checking service adds code to build, secure and operate, when IAP already does identity-based access natively.

  * **Option B: IAP for all services with allAuthenticatedUsers for public ones**  
`allAuthenticatedUsers` still requires every caller to sign in with a Google account, so the public services would not be unrestricted as the requirement asks. Putting IAP in front of services that should be open also adds configuration for no benefit.

  * **Option C: Use Cloud Endpoints with Firebase Authentication**  
Cloud Endpoints and Firebase Authentication can control access, but they need more setup than IAP, and Firebase Security Rules protect Firebase data, not Cloud Run services.




**Relevant Documentation:**

For more details, refer to:

  * [Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) Overview](https://cloud.google.com/iap/docs/concepts-overview)

  * [Cloud Run ingress settings](https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/securing/ingress)

**D. 1. Pub/Sub, 2. Dataflow, 3. Firestore, 4. BigQuery**

The diagram labels the steps: **1 = Ingest**, **2 = pipeline**, **3 = Transaction Databases**, **4 = Analytics**. Match each step to the service built for it:

  3. **Transaction Databases → Firestore.** An operational document database that the applications (GKE, App Engine, Compute Engine) read and write.

  4. **Analytics → BigQuery.** The data warehouse for SQL analysis. Dataflow streams into it directly.

  * **C** swaps the stores: BigQuery is an analytical warehouse, not a transactional database, and Firestore can't run the SQL analysis.

4-47.explanation:
**Correct Option:**

  * **III. Each developer creates a branch for their individual work, commits their changes to their branch, and merges their code into the main branch on a daily basis.**




**Justification:**

  * **Trunk-based development:** Google's DORA research (the "Trunk-based development" capability in Google Cloud's DevOps guidance) identifies short-lived branches merged into the main branch (trunk) at least once a day as a key predictor of high software delivery performance.

  * **Small, frequent merges:** Merging daily keeps each change small, so merge conflicts are rare and easy to resolve, and integration problems are found early by CI instead of right before a release.

  * **Fast feedback:** Combined with automated builds and tests on every merge, this keeps the main branch always releasable.




**Why Other Options Are Not Ideal:**

  * **I. Developers commit their code to the main branch before each product release...**

    * **Big-bang integration:** Code is integrated only before a release, so conflicts and integration bugs pile up and are found late, forcing rollbacks.

  * **II. Groups of developers copy the repository...**

    * **Long-lived forks:** Merging separate copies only before each release creates large, risky merges and extra coordination.

  * **IV. Groups of developers create a feature branch... following approval from the change advisory board.**

    * **Long-lived feature branches:** Feature branches that live until a release grow large and conflict-prone.

    * **Heavyweight approval:** DORA research found that approval by an external change advisory board slows delivery without improving stability. Lightweight peer review (for example, pull request review) is the recommended alternative.




**References:**

  * <https://cloud.google.com/architecture/devops/devops-tech-trunk-based-development>

  * <https://dora.dev/capabilities/trunk-based-development/>

  * <https://dora.dev/capabilities/streamlining-change-approval/>
4-47.why: Feature branches + change advisory board contradicts DORA/Google guidance; daily merges to main (trunk-based development) is the recommended practice and matches Exam 4 Q28.

4-6.explanation:
**Correct Answer:**

**III. Have the Cloud Build step write the Cloud Function results to a file and return 0. Add a step after the Cloud Function deletion that checks whether the file contains the expected results and fails if it doesn't.**

**Why:**

  * By default, Cloud Build stops the build as soon as a step fails, so a failing test step would skip the deletion step.

  * If the test step always returns 0 and records its outcome in a file, the deletion step always runs.

  * All steps share the `/workspace` directory, so the final step can read the file, check the results and fail the build if the test did not pass. Cleanup happens and the build still reports the test failure.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

  * **I.** Deleting the Cloud Function before the test means there is nothing left to test.

  * **II.** `waitFor` only controls ordering and parallelism. If the test step fails, the build still stops and the deletion step never runs.

  * **IV.** Environment variables set inside one step do not persist to later steps (each step runs in its own container), so the final step cannot read the outcome. Only files in `/workspace` are shared between steps.

**Note:** Cloud Build steps now also support `allowFailure` and `allowExitCodes`, which let the build continue after a failed test step. If such an option is offered, it is a cleaner design.

**Documentation:**

  * Build configuration file schema: <https://cloud.google.com/build/docs/build-config-file-schema>

  * Cloud Build: <https://cloud.google.com/build/docs/automating-builds/create-manage-triggers>

**IV. Establish a pull subscription with both ordering and exactly-once delivery disabled.**

Here's why:

  * **Pull for high volume:** A single large in-memory database is updated by subscribers that pull (ideally with StreamingPull) at their own pace. Pull subscriptions give the highest throughput and let the consumer control flow; push subscriptions are less suited to very large volumes.

  * **The timestamp makes ordering unnecessary:** Each message carries the stock symbol, price and timestamp, so the subscriber can simply keep the price with the newest timestamp for each symbol and ignore older ones. Ordering keys would only add latency and limit throughput.

  * **Duplicates are harmless:** Writing the same price for the same symbol and timestamp twice gives the same result (the update is idempotent), so exactly-once delivery isn't needed. Exactly-once delivery also adds significant publish-to-subscribe latency.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

  * **I. Pull with exactly-once enabled:** Works, but pays the extra latency and throughput cost of exactly-once delivery for no benefit, since duplicate updates are idempotent.

  * **II. Push with both disabled:** Push subscriptions are less suited to very high message volumes than pull, and the endpoint must absorb whatever rate Pub/Sub pushes.

  * **III. Push with exactly-once enabled:** Not possible. Exactly-once delivery is supported only on pull subscriptions (including StreamingPull); push and export subscriptions don't support it.

**References:**

<https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/exactly-once-delivery>

<https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/subscriber>

4-13.explanation:
**Correct Answer:**

**II. Create a pull subscription with both ordering and exactly-once delivery disabled.**

**Explanation:**

  * **The timestamp makes ordering unnecessary:** every message carries the stock symbol, the price and the time of that price. Before writing, the consumer compares the message's timestamp with the one stored for that symbol and ignores the message if it is older. An out-of-order message can never overwrite a newer price.

  * **Duplicates are harmless:** applying the same price with the same timestamp twice leaves the database unchanged, so the update is idempotent and exactly-once delivery adds nothing.

  * **Pull suits a stream of price updates:** a pull subscriber controls its own flow and can process messages in large batches, which suits a high, steady volume of updates. This is Google's own sample question for this exam, and its answer is a pull subscription with both features off.

  * **Leaving both features off keeps throughput and latency at their best:** ordering keys limit how messages for one key are dispatched, and exactly-once delivery adds acknowledgement overhead. Neither is needed here.




**Why Other Options Are Less Suitable:**

  * **I. Set up a push subscription with exactly-once delivery enabled.** Exactly-once delivery is supported only on pull subscriptions, so this combination isn't possible. It also wouldn't be needed, because duplicates are harmless here.

  * **III. Configure a pull subscription with ordering enabled, utilizing the stock symbol as the ordering key.** This works, but the timestamp already solves the ordering problem. Ordering keys add publisher-side requirements (the publisher must set the key, and per-key delivery is serialized), which only cost throughput.

  * **IV. Establish a push subscription with both ordering and exactly-once delivery disabled.** The feature settings are right, but push delivers each message as a separate HTTP request to an endpoint. For a high-volume stream of small updates, a pull subscriber that controls its own flow is the better fit.

**Remember:** If messages carry a timestamp or version, the consumer can discard stale updates itself, so you don't need ordering keys. Exactly-once delivery is a pull-only feature.
4-13.why: Keyed ordering by stock symbol, but the timestamp lets the consumer drop stale updates, so ordering isn't needed. Google's own sample question for this scenario keys a pull subscription with ordering and exactly-once both off; this also matches 4-26.

**III. Allocate the roles/storage.objectCreator role to the Cloud Function's runtime service account for the Cloud Storage bucket.**

Here's why this is the correct approach:

  * **Service Account Permissions:** Your function's code runs as its runtime service account (a dedicated service account you choose at deploy time, or the default one). That identity is what Cloud Storage checks, so it needs permission to write to the bucket in project B.

  * **Principle of Least Privilege:** Granting `roles/storage.objectCreator` on the bucket only provides the minimal permission required, limiting the potential security impact.

  * **Cross-Project Access:** The role is granted on the bucket in project B to a service account from project A, which is how cross-project access works.

  * **Not the service agent:** `service-PROJECT_NUMBER@gcf-admin-robot.iam.gserviceaccount.com` is the Cloud Functions *service agent*, which Google uses to manage your functions. Your code doesn't run as it, so granting it bucket access isn't the fix.

**Why Other Options are Not Ideal:**

  * **I. Grant your user account the roles/storage.objectCreator role ...** The function doesn't run as your user account, so this doesn't change what the function can do.

  * **II. Provide your user account with the roles/iam.serviceAccountUser ...** This lets you deploy functions that run as (act as) that service account, but doesn't give the service account any permission on the bucket.

  * **IV. Ensure the Cloud Storage API is enabled within project B** The bucket already exists and the error is a 403 permission error, so the API isn't the problem.

3-43.explanation:
**III. Implement signed URLs for file uploads.**

Explanation:

  * App Engine limits the size of an HTTP request to 32 MB, so a 500-MB file can't be uploaded through the App Engine app itself, multipart or not.

  * With **signed URLs**, the App Engine app authenticates the user and returns a time-limited URL that allows a PUT of one specific object in a Cloud Storage bucket. The client then uploads the file **directly to Cloud Storage**, which handles objects far larger than 500 MB. The app can still enforce the 500-MB limit (for example with an `x-goog-content-length-range` header in the signed URL) and keeps the bytes out of its instances.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

I. Utilize FTP for uploading files.

  * App Engine doesn't offer FTP access, and running your own FTP server adds security and operational work.

II. Use CPanel for file uploads.

  * cPanel is a control panel for traditional web hosting and has no role in App Engine.

IV. Modify the API to function as a multipart file upload API.

  * Multipart encoding only changes how the request body is formatted. The whole request still passes through App Engine and still hits its 32-MB request limit.

**References:**

<https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls>

<https://cloud.google.com/appengine/docs/standard/quotas#Requests>

6-13.explanation:
The approach that gives customers immediate confirmation is:

**D. Send the seat reservation as an HTTP POST request to an Application Load Balancer, which distributes it to a Compute Engine managed instance group that processes the reservation.**

**Explanation:**

  * **Immediate confirmation needs a synchronous call:** The customer has to know right away whether *their specific seat* was reserved. With a synchronous HTTP request, the backend checks and reserves the seat (for example in a transactional database) and returns success or "seat taken" in the same response.

  * **Scalability and availability:** The Application Load Balancer spreads requests across a managed instance group that autoscales during busy on-sale periods and replaces unhealthy instances.

**Why other options are not suitable:**

  * **A. Cloud Tasks and Workflow:** Queuing the request makes processing asynchronous. The client only learns that the task was queued, not whether the seat was reserved.

  * **B. Pub/Sub and Eventarc:** Publishing is asynchronous too. Pub/Sub acknowledges that it *received the message*, not that the seat was reserved, so the customer can't get an immediate reservation result (and the seat might already be taken when the message is processed).

  * **C. Cloud Storage:** Writing an object and reacting to the storage event is asynchronous and adds latency, so there's no immediate answer for the customer.

explanation: The committed stream type ensures that data written to BigQuery is immediately visible to queries and that each write operation is atomic. The BigQuery Storage Write API handles duplicate checks internally, making it a straightforward solution to avoid duplicate entries without additional infrastructure or deduplication logic.

In committed type, records are available for reading as soon as each write is acknowledged, and every append can carry a **stream offset**. If a write is retried with an offset that was already written, the API rejects it with an `ALREADY_EXISTS` error instead of writing the rows again, which gives **exactly-once** semantics without additional infrastructure or deduplication logic.

The default stream type is **buffered** , which means data is not immediately visible and requires a flush operation to make it available in BigQuery. Buffered streams are more prone to duplicates because they don’t enforce atomic writes as the committed type does.

The default stream gives **at-least-once** semantics: it doesn't support stream offsets, so a retried write can be written twice and produce duplicates. (Buffered is a separate stream type, in which rows become visible only after a flush.)
4-11.why: Default stream is at-least-once (not buffered); committed type avoids duplicates via stream offsets, not internal duplicate checks.

4-14.explanation:
**The most likely solution is:**

**IV. Utilize Cloud Scheduler in conjunction with Pub/Sub to invoke Cloud Run.**

**Explanation:**

  * **Cloud Scheduler:** The managed Google Cloud service for running jobs on a schedule. A Cloud Scheduler job publishes a message to a Pub/Sub topic on each run.

  * **Pub/Sub:** A **push subscription** on that topic delivers each message to the Cloud Run service as an authenticated HTTP request. Pub/Sub push is one of the Google Cloud sources that Cloud Run accepts with **internal** ingress (when it's in the same project or VPC Service Controls perimeter), so you keep the internal ingress setting. Give the push subscription's service account the **`roles/run.invoker`** role on the service; a missing invoker role is the usual cause of a 403 when calling Cloud Run.

**Why Other Options Might Not Be the Best Fit:**

  * **I. Assign the roles/run.developer IAM role to the service account.** `roles/run.developer` is for deploying and managing services, which is broader than needed. Invoking a service needs `roles/run.invoker`.

  * **II. Set up a cron job on the Compute Engine VMs to trigger Cloud Run based on the schedule.** While possible, it introduces more management overhead and potential points of failure compared to a managed service like Cloud Scheduler.

  * **III. Modify the Cloud Run ingress setting to 'Internal and Cloud Load Balancing.'** This loosens the internal ingress requirement and doesn't by itself fix the scheduling or the permission problem.

**References:**

<https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/triggering/using-scheduler>

<https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/securing/ingress>

4-16.explanation:
The **recommended approach is:**

✅ **II. Establish an Eventarc trigger to monitor your Cloud Storage bucket for a designated filename, with the target set as Cloud Run.**

✅ **Explanation for Correct Option:**

  * **Eventarc** routes many kinds of events (direct Cloud Storage events such as `google.cloud.storage.object.v1.finalized`, Cloud Audit Logs events, Pub/Sub messages and more) to targets like **Cloud Run**, so different trigger types use the same mechanism.

  * Direct Cloud Storage triggers filter by **bucket** and event type. To react to one specific file, the Cloud Run service checks the object name in the event (or you can use a Cloud Audit Logs trigger, which supports a **path pattern** on the resource name).

  * Triggers are simple, declarative resources (`gcloud eventarc triggers create/update`), so several team members can update them easily.

**Official Documentation:**

  * <https://cloud.google.com/eventarc/docs>

  * <https://cloud.google.com/run/docs/tutorials/eventarc>

❌ **Explanation for Incorrect Options:**

**I. Cloud Storage → Pub/Sub → Cloud Build**

  * Cloud Build is a **CI/CD** service, not a runtime for your application, and chaining three services is harder to maintain.

**III. Cloud Function triggered by Cloud Storage**

  * This works for a single fixed event source, but Eventarc routing to Cloud Run is the more flexible option when trigger types vary. (Event-driven Cloud Run functions, formerly Cloud Functions 2nd gen, use Eventarc triggers under the hood.)

**IV. Firebase Functions with Cloud Storage**

  * Firebase functions are aimed at Firebase-based apps and add a separate toolchain. This option is not recommended unless the application is built on Firebase.

**Summary:**

| Option | Verdict | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| I | ❌ | Cloud Build is CI/CD, not a runtime; chaining three services is harder to maintain |
| II | ✅ | One trigger mechanism for many event types; simple, declarative configuration |
| III | ❌ | Fine for one fixed event source, less flexible when trigger types vary |
| IV | ❌ | Firebase-specific, not meant for general Cloud Storage triggers |

4-41.explanation:
**C. Return an HTTP 500 Internal Server Error response.**

**Explanation:**

  * The question asks how to make sure your API's consumers are **notified** of the failure. Returning **HTTP 500** clearly tells them a server-side error occurred: their request was likely valid, but the server couldn't complete it, so they can retry later or report it.

  * It's still good practice to retry transient 5xx errors from Firestore internally with **bounded** exponential backoff first. If the write still fails after a limited number of attempts, return the 500.

**Why Other Options are Wrong:**

  * **A. Return an HTTP 204 No Content response.** A 204 response means success, which would mislead API consumers into thinking the write worked.

  * **B. Return an HTTP 406 Not Acceptable response.** A 406 response indicates a content-negotiation problem with the client's request, not a server-side failure.

  * **D. Retry the Datastore API with exponential backoff until Firestore returns an HTTP 2xx response.** Retrying without a limit never notifies the consumer, and the request can hang indefinitely during a longer outage. Retries help, but they don't replace reporting the failure.

**Documentation:**

  * **HTTP Status Codes:** <https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status>

  * **Retry strategy:** <https://cloud.google.com/datastore/docs/concepts/errors>

The recommended approaches for ensuring proper authentication of services accessing various Google Cloud APIs within a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster are:

**II. Enable Workload Identity Federation for GKE on the cluster through the gcloud command-line tool, establishing a secure mechanism for workloads operating in the cluster to access Google Cloud services with fine-grained IAM permissions.**

Explanation:

  * Option II enables Workload Identity Federation for GKE (formerly called Workload Identity) on the cluster, which is Google's recommended way for GKE workloads to access Google Cloud APIs with fine-grained IAM permissions, without managing service account keys.

  * Option V is the second half of the same setup: granting `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser` on the Google service account to the Kubernetes service account lets Pods that use that Kubernetes service account act as the Google service account. (You can also grant IAM roles directly to the Kubernetes service account as a principal.)

Options I, III, and IV are not recommended best practices:

  * Option I uses the service account linked to the GKE node. Every Pod on the node shares it, so it lacks granularity and breaks least privilege.

  * Options III and IV keep Google service account keys in Secret Manager. They are still long-lived keys that must be stored, rotated and protected, which Workload Identity Federation for GKE avoids.

**References:**

<https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/workload-identity>
